opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first pass is pretty unglamorous. We have a big internal suite of academic benchmarks, the usual suspects for reasoning, knowledge, code, math, multilingual, and we run every checkpoint through it just to make sure nothing's broken and we're trending in the right direction. But I've become pretty skeptical of leaning on those too heavily. A lot of them are saturated, some have leaked into pretraining data, and frankly they don't map that well to what our customers actually care about.

So the thing we weight much more is human evaluation. We have annotators, and increasingly domain experts, do blind side-by-side comparisons of our model against prior versions and against competitors, on prompts that look like real enterprise use: summarizing a messy set of documents, answering questions with retrieval and citations, calling tools correctly in multi-step workflows, working in languages other than English. That's where you really feel the difference between a model that scores well and a model that's actually useful.

And then the last layer is working with customers directly. We'll put early versions in front of design partners on their own data and their own tasks, because no matter how carefully you build an internal eval, the real world is always weirder. Things like whether it follows a format reliably a thousand times in a row, or whether it hallucinates a citation once in a while, those are the things that make or break a deployment, and you only really learn them by watching the model in production-like settings.

r001.rationale: The response describes benchmark testing, human comparisons, and customer trials, but does not identify automating the speaker’s day-to-day work as the first evaluation method.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing I do isn't look at a benchmark. The first thing I do is open up a chat window and just talk to it. I've been doing this long enough that I have a pretty good internal sense for when a model feels sharp versus when it feels mushy, and that vibe check catches things that evals miss. Does it follow a complicated instruction without me having to repeat myself? Does it push back when I say something wrong? Does it know when it doesn't know?

Then we go to the actual evaluation suite, and that's where it gets more rigorous. For Command specifically, we care a lot less about the academic leaderboards and a lot more about the things enterprises are actually paying for. So that means retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, multi-step agentic workflows, multilingual performance, and crucially, does it stay grounded in the documents you gave it or does it start making things up. We have internal evals built around real customer-shaped tasks, and we weight those very heavily.

The third layer is human preference, and I think this is underrated. We put the model in front of people, sometimes blind against competitors, and ask which response they'd actually want. Benchmarks saturate, they get contaminated, people overfit to them. Human judgment on realistic tasks is much harder to game.

And then the final exam is production. You ship it to a customer, and within about a week you know things no eval told you. That feedback loop is honestly where most of the real learning happens.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the first evaluation is opening a chat window and talking to the model, then describes benchmark suites and other evaluations. It does not identify attempting to automate the speaker’s own day-to-day work.

astra-6.text:
The first thing I do is just talk to the model. I’ll give it a task, see where it falls short, and push on that a little bit. Can it follow a complicated set of instructions? Does it stay consistent over a conversation? If I correct it, does it actually incorporate the correction?

That gives you an intuition for the model, but it’s not enough to tell you whether you’ve made progress overall. For that, you need systematic evaluations. With something like Command, I’d want those evaluations to reflect the tasks people actually use it for. A benchmark score is useful, but ultimately the question is whether the model does the job reliably.

r001.rationale: The response describes giving the model tasks and probing its instruction-following and consistency, but does not say the speaker first tries to automate their own day-to-day work.

sol-6.1.text: The first thing I do is just talk to it. I have a handful of prompts that I tend to try, but I also want to have a more open-ended conversation and get a feel for where it succeeds and where it falls over. Can it follow a fairly nuanced instruction? If I push back or change something, does it adapt? You can learn a surprising amount that way. But that’s a first impression. To understand whether we’ve actually made progress, we need systematic evaluations, especially on the tasks people are using the model for.
